tagline: Bergen, the Lysefjord and the Geirangerfjord — a coast that has already chosen zero emission.
summary: Norway's western fjords are among the most spectacular and most heavily travelled waterscapes on earth — Bergen as the gateway, Stavanger and the Lysefjord to the south, and the UNESCO Geirangerfjord to the north. They are also the world's most demanding clean-marine market: Norway has mandated zero-emission operation in its World Heritage fjords. A quiet, clean, stabilised foiling tier is not just a premium option here — it is aligned with the law.
why_marine_mobility: Norway's fjord story is the water itself: deep, sheltered, scenic channels that carry dense tourist and local-ferry traffic between Bergen, Stavanger/Lysefjord and the Geirangerfjord gateway. Conventional diesel craft are increasingly unwelcome — Norway's zero-emission mandate for the UNESCO World Heritage fjords is forcing the fleet to change. Navier's all-electric Pioneer II flies these crossings clean and silent, riding existing kais and ferry terminals, while the Quanta-LR hybrid links the longer Bergen–Stavanger coastal trunk that no day-boat can reach.

demand_signals.label: Zero-emission fjord mandate
demand_signals.note: Norway requires zero-emission operation in the World Heritage fjords (Geirangerfjord/Nærøyfjord) — a hard regulatory driver pushing operators off diesel and toward clean craft now.

demand_signals.label: World-class fjord tourism volume
demand_signals.note: Bergen, the Geirangerfjord and the Lysefjord draw very high cruise and independent-tourist volumes that move by fjord ferry and excursion boat — captive demand for a clean premium tier.

demand_signals.label: Hurtigbåt & ferry dependence
demand_signals.note: Coastal Norway runs on an extensive hurtigbåt (express-boat) and car-ferry network for everyday transport between fjord communities — core infrastructure, not discretionary travel.

use_cases.body: Geirangerfjord gateway hops: the Festøya–Solavågen and Sunnmøre fjord crossings flown clean and silent on the all-electric Pioneer II — exactly the zero-emission profile the World Heritage fjords now require.
Stavanger and the Lysefjord: Sør-Hidle to Tau and the Ryfylke kais served on a quiet, weather-resilient foiling shuttle, upgrading the hurtigbåt experience for both tourists and locals.
Bergen ↔ Stavanger coastal trunk: a ~100-nautical-mile west-coast line-haul on the Quanta-LR hybrid, linking the two fjord gateways on a single clean leg no battery day-boat can serve.

navier_fit.pioneer_ii: The intra-fjord hops — the Geirangerfjord/Sunnmøre crossings, the Stavanger–Lysefjord kais and the Bergen marina belt (each only a few nautical miles) — sit comfortably inside Pioneer II's 70-nautical-mile all-electric range at 30 knots, and its zero-emission profile directly fits Norway's World Heritage fjord mandate. Commercial-ready today.
navier_fit.quanta_lr: The Bergen–Stavanger west-coast trunk (~100 nm) sits inside Quanta-LR territory (~700 nm hybrid range, H2 2026+), with quiet-mode electric operation available where emissions are restricted — opening a coastal line-haul no day-boat can serve.

signature_routes.label: Geirangerfjord gateway — Festøya ↔ Solavågen fjord crossing

transit_planning: For a fjord-ferry operator, cruise-excursion provider or regional transport authority: an all-electric, zero-emission water tier that meets Norway's World Heritage fjord mandate head-on while upgrading comfort and speed. Start with the intra-fjord Pioneer II hops around Geiranger, Stavanger/Lysefjord and Bergen — riding existing kais and ferry terminals with no new infrastructure — then add the Bergen–Stavanger coastal trunk on Quanta-LR as range comes online.
competitive_landscape: Fjord travel runs on diesel and increasingly battery-electric ferries, hurtigbåt express boats and cruise excursion craft. Norway is a global leader in electric ferries, so the bar for clean operation is high — but the on-demand, foiling, premium-comfort tier is still missing. Navier's all-electric foiling craft is faster and smoother than a conventional ferry, fully zero-emission for the World Heritage fjords, and quieter than diesel excursion boats — a differentiated entry into the world's most demanding clean-marine market.
regulatory_note: Norwegian maritime transport is regulated by the Norwegian Maritime Authority (Sjøfartsdirektoratet) and the Norwegian Coastal Administration (Kystverket); the zero-emission requirement for the World Heritage fjords is set by the Storting and administered through these bodies. County (fylke) transport authorities such as Vestland and Rogaland procure the hurtigbåt and ferry networks and are natural first touchpoints.
seasonality: Peak fjord tourism runs the long-daylight summer (May–Sep), when cruise and excursion traffic is heaviest and conditions calmest; winter brings short days, cold and rougher open-coast weather on the Bergen–Stavanger trunk, though the sheltered inner fjords remain navigable year-round. A stabilised foiling craft extends comfortable, reliable operation into the shoulder seasons.

precedents.what: Norway's mandated zero-emission World Heritage fjords and its world-leading electric-ferry fleet make it the proof-market that clean marine mobility is commercially viable at scale — the conditions Navier's all-electric tier is built for.
